RPG Maker since XP uses the scripting language Ruby (each version uses different builds of Ruby, make sure to make your code along the same code guidelines for the Ruby build each engine uses). RPG Maker MV (newest one, currently not out yet, will use Javascript)

General overview of each available legal maker

RPG Maker 2000: Very basic, no Ruby scripting, but is great for making nostalgic NES/SNES style RPGs.

RPG Maker 2003: An updated version of 2000, most of the same applies.

RPG Maker XP: First version to include Ruby scripting, uses a larger tileset than most of the other makers.

RPG Maker VX: Uses an updated Ruby scripting module, tilesets are smaller, though the engine is heavily based on XP, so a lot of features will be familiar.

RPG Maker VX Ace: An updated version of VX. Features an even more recent Ruby scripting module, has more features than VX, latest currently available RPG Maker engine.

RPG Maker MV; Uses Javascript instead of Ruby for cross platform compatibility, works on Windows/Mac/Linux/Android (the games made for it can be somewhat easily be cross platformed for these environments), and features many features from XP and 2003 bolted onto an enhanced VX Ace like base. Database limit has been doubled since VX/ACE, from 999 to 2000 items for all categories. Features a slighty upscaled VX/ACE styled tileset schema.

Note: Some of the makers have compatibility issues with Windows 10, though XP and later should work well if you use the Compatibility Manager to determine what the best settings are. 2000/2003 have keyboard issues at present, check the above forums for possible fixes.

Use of Wine can emulate these engines in Linux quite well, similar results can be achieved on Macs.

Finally, even if you don't use certain engines, you may wish to purchase them anyway. Due to the EULA terms for each engine, resources meant for one engine may not be ported to another unless you have a license to use the engine the resources were meant for, so owning more than one engine can expand the amount of resources available for use.

I think that gaming as an industry is moving farther into the cloud because of the control that it gives publishers and to a lesser extent, developers. Devs can enforce patches on players and make sure everyone is up to date. They can also count on releasing a game and finishing it later because of the expectation of a good internet connection. Physical media isn't physical media anymore when almost every game you buy requires a multiple gigabite update. Publishers get to push their networks on players, and leverage those networks to control who has access to their game. It's been a trend for a while now, and I don't think that the convenience of digital downloads and saved content libraries are worth the power we're losing as consumers. We don't hold the cards we used to. Right now we're playing them from the publisher's hands.
